evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work individual contributor roles with low autonomy]

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2015). Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(1), 165-218. — This landmark field experiment on call center workers (low autonomy roles) provides causal evidence on remote work productivity, directly relevant to testing the hypothesis for low-autonomy individual contributors.

[PATH:empirical] Gibbs, M., Mengel, F., & Siemroth, C. (2023). Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from a Software Firm. Journal of Labor Economics, 41(4), 987-1025. — This study examines productivity effects of remote work in a technology firm, differentiating by task autonomy and role type, offering evidence on whether low-autonomy roles see decreased output.

[PATH:empirical] Choudhury, P., Foroughi, C., & Larson, B. (2021). Work-from-Anywhere: The Productivity Effects of Geographic Flexibility. Strategic Management Journal, 42(4), 655-683. — This research analyzes remote work productivity in professional services, including variation by worker autonomy, and can help confirm or refute the hypothesis for the specified domain and time period.

[PATH:empirical] Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2015). 'Does Working from Home Work? Evidence from a Chinese Experiment.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(1), 165-218. — This field experiment with a large tech firm provides causal evidence on remote work productivity, including for high-autonomy roles. Re-analyzing its subgroup effects could confirm or refute decreased per-worker output for such roles.

[PATH:empirical] Choudhury, P., Foroughi, C., & Larson, B. (2021). 'Work-from-Anywhere: The Productivity Effects of Geographic Flexibility.' Strategic Management Journal, 42(4), 655-683. — This study examines productivity in a fully remote, high-autonomy setting (US Patent Office). Its findings on output changes under high autonomy can directly test the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Gibbs, M., Mengel, F., & Siemroth, C. (2023). 'Work from Home and Productivity: Evidence from a Software Firm.' Journal of Labor Economics, 41(4), 899-938. — Using granular data from a tech firm, this paper analyzes how remote work affects individual contributor output, especially for roles with high autonomy. It can provide evidence on the disputed direction of the effect.

qualifier.geographic: United States, Western Europe, and Australia

C007.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work teams requiring frequent ad-hoc coordination]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing productivity of co-located vs. remote teams in high-interdependence product development tasks, measuring task completion time and error rates under ad-hoc coordination scenarios — Directly tests the causal claim by manipulating the key variable (remote vs. co-located) in a setting that matches the hypothesis's scope and qualifier, providing high internal validity.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study using digital trace data (e.g., Slack/Teams message frequency, response times, task handoff logs) from knowledge-economy firms post-2020, correlated with individual productivity metrics (e.g., output per hour) and controlling for team interdependence — Leverages naturalistic data in the specified temporal and geographic context to observe real-world patterns, addressing external validity and the role of ad-hoc coordination frequency.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on remote work productivity, focusing on studies that report interaction effects between team interdependence and coordination modality (synchronous vs. asynchronous, high-bandwidth tools) — Synthesizes available evidence to assess overall effect size and consistency across contexts, identifying gaps and moderators that could confirm or refute the hypothesis.

scope.domain: industries with high interdependence (e.g., product development with tight integration)

qualifier.temporal: since widespread adoption of high-bandwidth remote collaboration tools (post-2020)
qualifier.geographic: global, primarily in knowledge-economy regions with reliable internet infrastructure

C008.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work teams requiring frequent ad-hoc coordination]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study comparing ad-hoc coordination outcomes (e.g., time-to-resolve, output quality) between co-located and remote teams in high-interdependence product development firms, controlling for communication tool quality over 6-12 months. — Directly tests the hypothesis in the specified domain and timeframe, providing causal evidence on whether remote work increases collaborative output for teams needing frequent ad-hoc coordination.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on remote work and team coordination, focusing on effect size of ad-hoc collaboration in high-interdependence settings (e.g., software engineering, R&D). — Synthesizes available evidence to assess the overall direction and strength of the relationship, identifying moderators like communication tool quality and task interdependence.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling the dynamics of ad-hoc coordination in remote vs. co-located teams, varying communication latency, tool quality, and task interdependence. — Explores mechanisms underlying the hypothesis, such as information flow and spontaneous interaction, and predicts conditions under which remote work might increase or decrease output, guiding empirical design.

scope.domain: industries with high interdependence (e.g., product development with tight integration)

qualifier.context: 6–12 month period, controlling for communication tool quality
